grades.summary: The selection model itself (src/model/selection.ts) is clean and sound: a small observable store of Element refs plus a transform-aware overlay renderer. The transform tools, however, are riddled with coordinate-space confusion between an element's LOCAL attribute space and DOC space, and they special-case "single un-transformed element" everywhere, so anything with a pre-existing transform (PDF-imported matrix(), translated/scaled groups, rotated shapes) gets corrupted or jumps. The worst offenders are: free-transform rotate silently dropping translate/scale from a matrix transform (data corruption), reflect using a doc-space AABB center against local-space coordinates for transformed elements (mirror placed wrong), and multi-select scale ignoring per-element transforms. The undo/redo plumbing (reset-then-execute via ModifyAttributeCommand) is correct and consistent across both tools, selection is properly cleared after Delete, and INPUT/TEXTAREA focus is guarded in every keyboard path — so the historical focus-stealing and stale-ref fault-lines do NOT recur here. This is fixable, not a rewrite: the bugs are concentrated in a handful of transform-composition spots that all share the same root cause (mixing local and doc coordinate frames). A single helper that consistently maps anchor/center/mouse into the element's local space before mutating local attributes would kill most of them.
grades.arch: The design is fundamentally sound and under-engineered in the good sense: selection is a tiny observable store of live DOM Element references with a RAF-coalesced overlay renderer, and all mutations route through ModifyAttributeCommand/CompoundCommand using a disciplined reset-then-execute pattern that makes undo/redo correct and uniform across both tools. The historical fault-lines the owner worries about are NOT present here — INPUT/TEXTAREA focus is guarded in every keyboard handler (Canvas, EditorContext, useToolShortcuts), Delete clears selection so no stale refs survive, and _-prefixed params (_getDoc) are genuinely unused pass-throughs. The real architectural weakness is the absence of a single coordinate-frame abstraction: every transform operation hand-rolls local-vs-doc-space mapping and special-cases "single untransformed element," which is why the same class of bug (doc-space anchor/center applied to local-space attributes) recurs in selectTool scale, reflect, and free-transform. selectTool and freeTransformTool also duplicate ~70% of their scale/rotate/commit logic with subtle divergences (findings 1, 8, 9). Testability is decent for the pure model layer (selection.ts, matrix.ts, reflect.ts have unit tests) but the tools are DOM/event-heavy and only validated via the dogfood/golden suites; the transform-composition bugs above are exactly the kind unit tests should pin down. Recommendation: extract one toLocalFrame(el, point) helper and one composeTransform(el, matrix) helper, route both tools and reflect through them, and the bug list collapses to two or three fixes rather than a rewrite.

grades.summary: This subsystem has a fundamental architectural fracture: the node editor (directSelectTool) ships its OWN regex-based path parser/serializer that is incompatible with the robust parsePathD/commandsToD parser used by every other tool (selectTool, freeTransform, knife, join, PDF export, reflect, grafting). The directSelect parser silently mishandles relative commands (m/l/c treated as absolute), ignores H/V/S/Q/T/A entirely, and drops them on the floor when rebuilding the d string — so direct-selecting any path that came from an imported SVG, a non-path auto-conversion, or its own auto-convert-to-path flow will corrupt or destroy geometry. On top of that there are concrete data-loss interlocks: the auto-convert-to-path flow holds a stale element ref across undo, and several edge-case math/serialization bugs in pathOps. The pen tool is the most solid piece. The DI-by-getter design and the pure functions are testable (and tested), but the existing tests only ever feed absolute, space-separated, M/L/C input — they validate the happy path the parser was written against, which is exactly why the corruption bugs survived. This is fixable but the node editor must be rebuilt on top of parsePathD; do not salvage the bespoke parser.
grades.arch: The design is reasonable on paper: tools are factories taking getter injections (getSvg/getDoc/getHistory), edits go through a command/history layer, and the core geometry (pathOps, pathSimplify, pen buildPathD) is pure and unit-tested. The fatal flaw is duplication of the single most important primitive: there are TWO path parsers with different capabilities and different coordinate assumptions, and the powerful one (parsePathD, which normalizes relative/H/V/S/Q/T/A to absolute M/L/C/Z) is NOT the one the node editor uses. That is the root cause of the worst findings and the source of cross-tool interlock corruption (convert-to-path then node-edit destroys geometry). It is under-engineered where it matters (node editor parser) and not over-engineered elsewhere. Testability is good structurally but the existing tests are a false comfort — they only feed absolute, well-spaced M/L/C input, which is precisely the subset the buggy parser handles, so they pass while real imported/converted paths break. Recommendation: keep penTool and pathOps, rebuild the directSelect node editor entirely on top of parsePathD/commandsToD, add tests with relative + H/V/S/Q/T/A + compound-path fixtures, and add node-level Delete/Escape handling.

grades.summary: The shape tools (rect, ellipse, line, pencil, eyedropper) are genuinely solid: a clean, consistent factory pattern with getSvg/getDoc/getHistory closures, preview elements tagged data-role="preview" (correctly stripped on export/save), grid+point snapping, locked-layer guards, and a uniform "create -> select -> switch to select tool" finish. They do not warrant a rewrite. The rot is concentrated in the text subsystem and a couple of cross-module interlocks. The worst issue is a keyboard interlock: while the text tool holds keyboard capture, EditorContext deliberately lets ALL Ctrl combos through (line 63: `if (isKeyboardCaptured() && !e.ctrlKey) return`), so Ctrl+Z/C/V/X/D/G/A fire global document operations mid-text-edit instead of being suppressed — exactly the historical "inputs swallowing shortcuts" fault, inverted. The text tool also commits a hardcoded 16-unit font into an mm document space (A4 = 210x297mm), producing a ~16mm-tall glyph (~45pt) for every text object. The eraser's multi-element undo can throw NotFoundError when erased siblings are restored out of order. areaText.ts is dead, unwired code with incoherent mm/px units. Hand-rolled text caret/selection/measurement is the under-tested, high-maintenance liability; a staff engineer would not approve the text path as-is, but everything else is shippable after targeted fixes.
grades.arch: The factory-per-tool pattern (closures over getSvg/getDoc/getHistory, a ToolConfig with handlers + onDeactivate, registry-driven dispatch) is sound, consistent, and genuinely testable for the shape tools — pointInPolygon, measureDistance, snapLineAngle, computeRect/computeEllipse are pure and unit-test-friendly. Preview lifecycle (data-role='preview' + central OVERLAY_SELECTOR stripping in fileio) is a clean separation of editor chrome from document. The two real architecture smells are: (1) keyboard ownership is split across Canvas.tsx and EditorContext.tsx with capture gating that leaks Ctrl combos (finding 1) — keyboard routing should be a single dispatcher that respects capture wholesale; (2) the text tool reimplements a text editor (caret blink, selection ranges, substring measurement) by hand against raw SVG, which is the under-tested, high-bug-density part and the main argument for reworking specifically the text path (e.g. a contentEditable/foreignObject or a dedicated text-edit model). Units are a latent hazard: the codebase is mm-native but font sizes and areaText assume px without conversion. Verdict: keep and harden the shape tools; rework the text subsystem and delete areaText.ts. This is a fix-this-part situation, not a full rewrite.

grades.summary: The in-scope modules are individually small, clean, and well-tested — registry.ts, defaultStyle.ts, markers.ts and guides.ts are each tidy singletons with a swap-the-active-instance pattern that supports multi-document. This is NOT rewrite territory. The real defects live at the INTERLOCK boundary, not inside these files: keyboard input is dispatched by THREE independent uncoordinated window keydown listeners (useToolShortcuts, Canvas, EditorContext), and the only coordination mechanism is the single boolean `keyboardCaptured`. That boolean is too coarse: during text editing it correctly suppresses single-key tool shortcuts but deliberately lets Ctrl-combos through to EditorContext, so Ctrl+Z/X/V/C while typing operate on the document/selection instead of the text — a genuine chained-failure bug. Separately, two of the in-scope files (the `ToolConfig.icon` field and the entire iconKeyForTool module) are dead in production: LeftRail hardcodes its own icon keys AND its own shortcut letters, so the registry's icon/shortcut data and the visible UI can silently drift. guides.ts has an asymmetric reset() that wipes subscribers without notifying. Nothing here loses or corrupts a saved document, hence B not C/D — but the keyboard interlock is a real user-facing footgun and the dead-code/drift is exactly the kind of rot that makes an owner want to rewrite.
grades.arch: The core design is sound and intentional: each concern (registry, default style, guides, markers) is a tiny module-singleton with a getActive/setActive-instance swap so multiple documents can each own their own state bundle, wired centrally in documentState.setActiveDocument. That pattern is clean, testable (every file has a focused test), and not over-engineered. The weakness is not inside these files — it is the absence of a single keyboard-input owner. Input handling is smeared across three window listeners coordinated only by one coarse boolean (keyboardCaptured), which is structurally why the text-edit Ctrl-combo bug exists and why guard logic is duplicated and already inconsistent. Secondary rot: the registry carries icon and shortcut data that the actual UI (LeftRail) duplicates by hand, so the registry is the source of truth in name only and two whole units (ToolConfig.icon, iconKeyForTool) are dead. Recommendation: keep the modules, centralize keyboard dispatch, and either make LeftRail consume the registry or delete the unused fields — a few days of focused work, not a rewrite.

grades.summary: This subsystem is competently structured but has a cluster of real interlock/undo defects concentrated in gradient handling and transform editing. The dominant problem is that gradient creation mutates the document <defs> OUTSIDE the command/history system, so undo/redo and document state desync, and every fill-type toggle leaks an orphan gradient. Transform editing in the ControlBar can silently destroy a baked matrix (scale/translate) when rotation is set to 0. The color/default-style plumbing and the controlled-input pattern are sound and well-tested-looking. Nothing here is unsalvageable; the bugs are localized and fixable without a rewrite, but they are exactly the "feature A leaves state that breaks feature B (undo)" class the owner is worried about.
grades.arch: The design is reasonable and mostly testable: a single source of truth (the live SVG DOM), a thin command/history layer (ModifyAttributeCommand/CompoundCommand) with a clean undo/redo stack, pub/sub for selection + default-style + history-tick re-derivation, and a consistent controlled-input pattern (local editing state synced on blur, Escape-to-revert) reused in both panels. Testid hooks and the milestone comments show genuine test discipline. The core flaw is a leaky abstraction boundary: not all document mutations go through the history layer — gradient <defs> creation (and to a lesser degree direct setAttribute in a few handlers) sidesteps it, which is precisely what produces the undo desync and the defs leak. PropertiesPanel.tsx is also overgrown (~725 lines, deeply nested IIFEs returning JSX) and duplicates frame/transform logic that already exists in ControlBar; consolidating the per-tag geometry math into one shared module would shrink both and remove the path/g read-only-input divergence. Verdict: salvageable — enforce 'every document mutation is a Command', add a defs GC / gradient-reuse pass, fix the matrix-clear, and de-duplicate the geometry, and this subsystem reaches B/A without a rewrite.

grades.summary: The shell architecture is fundamentally reasonable: a thin React layer over imperative DOM/SVG singletons, with a command-history undo stack and a per-document state bundle that anticipates multi-doc. Coordinate math (screenToDoc via getScreenCTM) is correct and reflect bakes transforms into geometry to avoid leftover scale() matrices — both are signs of a developer who learned from past fault-lines. However the subsystem carries several real, user-visible interlock bugs: Document Setup is silently broken (dialog updates React state but never the artboard model that Canvas actually reads), the ruler drag-to-guide feature emits guides on the wrong coordinate axis (X used as a horizontal guide's Y, and vice versa), keyboard shortcuts fire while a Properties-panel <select> is focused because the input guard only covers INPUT/TEXTAREA, and Shift+Ctrl+' toggles grid visibility instead of snap due to branch-ordering. None are unfixable; the bones are sound enough that a rewrite is not warranted, but the owner's frustration is justified — these are exactly the chained-state failures they flagged, and they ship today. Testability is mediocre: the heavy reliance on module-level singletons and direct window listeners makes the routing logic hard to unit-test, which is why these bugs survived.
grades.arch: The design is a deliberate hybrid: React owns chrome/layout and the imperative SVG/DOM owns the document, with module-level singletons (selection, guides, artboard, grid, tool registry) plus a command-history undo stack. This is a sensible choice for a vector editor and the seams (DocumentState bundle, setActiveDocument) show genuine forethought toward multi-document. It is neither over- nor under-engineered for its size. The real weakness is testability and discipline around the singletons: event routing is spread across three independent window listeners (EditorContext, Canvas, useToolShortcuts) with implicit ordering and three slightly different input-focus guards, which is precisely why the <select> leak and the Document-Setup desync survived. The two most damaging bugs (app-shell-1, app-shell-2) are pure state-propagation/coordinate mistakes, not architectural rot — they are localized and cheap to fix. Recommend consolidating keyboard routing into a single dispatcher with one shared 'is editable target' predicate, and driving the Canvas viewBox from the artboard model rather than a parallel React `dimensions` prop, before considering anything more drastic.

grades.summary: This is a genuinely well-engineered subsystem, not a rewrite candidate. The modules are small, pure, single-responsibility, and heavily unit-tested (12 test files). The hard parts — redaction-before-font-registration ordering, the Y-flip round-trip through redaction, Identity-H TJ shaping with GPOS adjustments, font subsetting — are correct and the inline reasoning is unusually disciplined. The owner's frustration is more likely with FIDELITY GAPS than with broken architecture. The real defects cluster in two places: (1) the integration seam in fileio.ts/ensureFontIfNeeded only ever feeds Carlito-Regular, so all NEW bold/italic overlay text silently renders upright-regular even though the multi-slot registry that would fix it already exists and is tested; (2) the two transform-composition paths (walkLayer vs emitElementWithAncestors) disagree about whether a layer's OWN transform is applied, and graftCs drops group-inherited fill/stroke/opacity entirely. None of these corrupt the PDF or lose data; they produce visually-wrong output in specific cases. Grade B: ship-quality bones, with a handful of real correctness gaps to close.
grades.arch: The design is sound and notably disciplined: each module is pure and single-purpose (graftCs = op emission, graftBbox = AABBs, graftClassify = layer triage, graftMupdf = native lifecycle, graftShape = shaping, graftExport = orchestration), and the seams are clean enough that the heavy logic is unit-testable without spinning up a real PDF — borne out by the 12 graft*.test.ts files. The redaction-before-font-registration ordering and the redaction Y-flip round-trip are both correct and, more importantly, the WHY is documented inline, which is exactly what you want in a coordinate-space minefield. It is neither over- nor under-engineered for an MVP. The genuine weaknesses are at the integration boundary, not the core: fileio.ts hands the engine only Carlito-Regular (wasting the bold/italic infra that already exists and is tested), the two transform-composition paths disagree about layer-level transforms, SVG style inheritance (group fill/opacity) is unmodeled, and several coordinate assumptions (MediaBox origin = 0,0; text rotation) are unstated. Salvageability is high — these are targeted fixes, not a rewrite. Recommend NOT rewriting; instead close graft-engine-1/2/3 first, then the coordinate-assumption items.

grades.summary: The core architecture is sound and more disciplined than the owner fears: the worker boundary is clean, the SourcePdfStore/graft-vs-pdf-lib routing has a clear contract, coordinate conversions are mostly consistent (no double Y-flip in this path — drawText flips via svgPtToPdf, drawPath relies on drawSvgPath's internal flip, and the two never compound), and the export engine is deterministic and testable. What drags the grade down is a genuine state-leak interlock class: the SourcePdfStore is never cleared on the paths that logically invalidate it (Open SVG, layer delete, New Document), so stale ~10MB byte buffers and stale source-id mappings survive document changes. That's exactly the chained-failure category the owner flagged, and it's the most important thing to fix. The pdf-lib fallback engine also silently drops rotation, bold-serif, and most colors — wrong output rather than a crash. Debug console.log/console.warn spam is shipped in the hot path. None of this requires a rewrite; it's a focused cleanup pass.
grades.arch: The design is fundamentally sound and notably better than the 'consider a rewrite' framing suggests. The worker boundary (pdfRender.ts pure / pdfRender.worker.ts shim / pdfImport.ts pending-map) is clean, cancel-safe, and rejects all pending requests on worker death. Coordinate handling is the usual mm↔pt↔PDF-pt minefield but is actually consistent here: there is NO double Y-flip in this subsystem — drawText flips via svgPtToPdf while drawPath deliberately does not and leans on drawSvgPath's internal flip, and the comments document why. Leaf-vs-container transform handling is correctly applied to leaves in walk(). The real weakness is lifecycle/teardown discipline: SourcePdfStore has a clear contract on paper but its teardown half is dead code, so document-replacing and layer-deleting operations leave stale source state — the exact interlock class to fear, and the reason for the C. The pdf-lib fallback engine is honestly under-built (rotation/color/weight gaps) but it is self-aware about being MVP and is well isolated and testable (pure svgStringToPdfBytes, deterministic metadata pinning for golden byte-match). Testability overall is good (most functions exported for tests, pure pipelines). Recommendation: salvage, do not rewrite — fix the store teardown wiring first (pdf-io-1/2/10), then harden the pdf-lib primitive path (pdf-io-3/4/5).

grades.summary: This is competent, well-documented, mostly-pure model code. The three files are individually clean: tagging is trivially correct, font extraction handles the Type0-descendant and standard-14-null edge cases deliberately (with comments that match mupdf reality), and the snapshot/diff logic is sound for the attribute-only scope it claims. I found NO crash/corruption bug in the read paths. The real problems are INTERLOCK and dead-code issues: (1) an entire count-based deletion-detection API (expectedSourceCount/currentSourceCount/SOURCE_COUNT_ATTR) is dead — nothing in production calls it, yet snapshotImportedElements still stamps data-vf-source-count onto every imported layer, which then serializes into saved/exported SVG as junk metadata; (2) the documented 'text content tracked at Command level' contract is vaporware — commandTouchesSource is consumed nowhere outside commands.ts, and there is no text-content-edit command, so the moment Phase-3 in-place text editing lands, edited source text will silently classify as graft and be lost; (3) findRemovedElementBboxes uses layer.contains(el), so moving a source element to another layer is misreported as a deletion and gets masked over; (4) the snapshot WeakMap and registry are in-memory only and never rebuilt on SVG reload, so the whole edit-detection state is session-scoped (currently masked by the SourcePdfStore also being session-scoped, but a latent footgun). This is salvageable — none of it is rewrite-grade structural failure, it's accumulated half-wired features and stale doc-comments.
grades.arch: The decomposition is sound and genuinely testable: three single-responsibility pure modules (tagging = DOM attr stamps, font = mupdf-object reads, snapshot = WeakMap diff), each with a focused test file, no DOM mutation outside tagImportedLayer/snapshotImportedElements, no I/O. Edge-case handling in sourceFont.ts (Type0 descendant descent, standard-14 PDFObject.Null guards, WASM-slab copy-out) is unusually careful and the comments are accurate to mupdf behavior — this is the strongest file. The weakness is at the SEAMS, not inside the modules: the subsystem has two parallel, partly-dead deletion-detection mechanisms (count attr vs bbox registry), a documented-but-unwired text-content/Command contract, and several latent hardcodes (page 0, pageKey-vs-fontKey identity) that are correct only by accident of 'imports are always single-page page 0'. It is mildly over-engineered (WeakRef+UID registry, count attr) for what is currently exercised, and under-engineered on persistence (all edit-detection state is session-scoped and silently relies on the source store also being session-scoped). Verdict: keep all three modules, but prune the dead count API, fix the contains()-based removal and page-0 hardcodes, and either implement or delete the text-content/Command path before Phase-3 in-place editing lands.

grades.summary: This subsystem is the healthiest part of the app I have seen. The matrix math is correct (multiply/invert/apply/parseTransform all compose in the right SVG left-to-right order), the pub-sub state singletons (grid/wireframe/activeLayer/artboard/smartGuides) are clean and consistent, and the transform-aware AABB pipeline is genuinely the single source of truth it claims to be. There is no double-Y-flip, no leaf-vs-container confusion in the move path (computeTranslateAttrs and selectTool.moveElement both correctly compose T*M for groups and shift rotate-centers for attr-positioned shapes), and the smart-guide candidate cache lifecycle is correctly opened/closed around drags. The real defects are concentrated and mostly edge-case: decomposeMatrix mis-reports scaleY/skewX under shear; two rotate-center regexes disagree on scientific-notation support; smart-guide line emission has tie/dup quirks; and a handful of NaN-silently-propagating parse paths. None are data-loss or corrupt-export class. This does not need a rewrite — it needs a half-day of targeted fixes plus a few decompose/skew unit tests.
grades.arch: The design is sound and notably disciplined for a 25K-LOC editor: one affine Matrix type with pure functions, one transformedAABB used uniformly by hit-test, smart guides, align, and the control bar, and a consistent module pattern (private class + module-level `active` singleton + thin free-function facade + reset()) across grid/wireframe/activeLayer/artboard/smartGuides that makes per-document teardown trivial. It is testable — matrix.ts is pure and already has decent unit coverage (the decompose-with-shear gap is a test omission, not an architecture flaw); the geometry/DOM-touching functions are harder to unit test but are thin wrappers. Mild under-engineering risks: regex-based transform mutation is duplicated in at least five files with subtly different patterns (the geometry-rotate-regex finding) and should be centralized into matrix.ts helpers; coordinate units (mm vs px) are correct but enforced only by convention/comments, not types, so a typed Mm/Px brand would prevent a whole class of future mix-ups. Overall this subsystem does NOT justify a rewrite — it is the load-bearing, correct core; spend the effort hardening parse paths and consolidating the duplicated rotate-center regex instead.

grades.summary: The command/undo core (CommandHistory, the leaf command classes) is clean, small, and correctly structured — execute/undo are symmetric for the simple cases and the touchesSource() plumbing for the graft exporter is thoughtful. The rot is concentrated at the interlock seams, exactly where the owner feared: (1) paste leaks duplicate IDs into the document because only the top-level pasted element is re-ID'd while all transferred descendants keep their original ids, corrupting every subsequent id-based lookup; (2) GroupCommand mishandles cross-layer and out-of-DOM-order selections, so undoing a group moves elements to the wrong layer / wrong z-position; (3) no command in the subsystem restores selection on undo/redo, and the live selection array is never purged when elements are removed, leaving stale Element refs in selection state after cut/delete. None of these are crashes, but several are silent data/structure corruption that only surfaces later — classic chained-failure bugs. This is fixable without a rewrite; the architecture is sound, the bugs are localized.
grades.arch: The design is fundamentally sound and refreshingly small: a flat Command interface with symmetric execute/undo, a 200-entry CommandHistory with a clean subscribe/notify, and well-factored operation modules (clipboard/nudge/zOrder) that were deliberately extracted from EditorContext for testability — that intent is good and pays off. It is neither over- nor under-engineered for a single-document editor. The two structural weaknesses: (1) selection is treated as orthogonal to the command system, so no operation snapshots/restores selection and the selection array holds raw, never-purged Element references — selection lifecycle should be owned by CommandHistory (snapshot ids around execute/undo/redo) rather than scattered clearSelection() calls in callers. (2) DocumentState's pointer-swap multi-document scheme is elegant on paper but the subscriber model captures instances at subscribe time, so the advertised Phase-2 will break without a re-bind step. Testability is decent for the leaf commands (they take plain Elements + a DocumentModel) but the interlock bugs found here are precisely the ones unit tests miss — they need DOM-round-trip and cross-layer fixtures. Salvageable: fix the id-uniquification on paste, make Group capture per-child parent/sibling, and centralize selection in the history; no rewrite warranted.

grades.summary: This is presentational chrome that is mostly competent React, but it has a cluster of real interlock and correctness defects concentrated in LayersPanel, plus a fully dead theme subsystem. The two most damaging bugs: (1) layer visibility/lock toggles bypass the command history entirely, so hiding a layer is not undoable, never marks the doc dirty (status bar still says "Saved"), yet DOES affect export/serialize — a silent data-divergence trap; and (2) addLayer mutates DOM z-order OUTSIDE the AddElementCommand, so redo replays the element to the wrong stacking position. Layer rows are also displayed in raw DOM order (bottom-painted layer at the top of the list), inverting the universal design-tool convention, which makes the move-up/move-down arrows move layers the "wrong" way relative to z-order. The theme/atrium.ts file (4 palettes, ~70 LOC) has zero importers and CSS variables are hand-duplicated in index.css, so the file is dead weight that will silently drift. IconGlyph hardcodes a dark ink stroke color instead of currentColor, so active-tool color theming and any non-light palette are broken at the icon level. Nothing here justifies a full rewrite — the bugs are localized and the styling is consistent — but LayersPanel's state/command discipline needs a real pass.
grades.arch: The design altitude is right: small, mostly pure presentational components, a clean IconGlyph dictionary, and a sensible Panel primitive. The rot is in state discipline, not structure. LayersPanel is the weak link: it tracks the active layer by positional index into a stale-closure array AND drives a global module-singleton (activeLayer) that every drawing/clipboard tool reads via getActiveLayer() — so the panel is a high-traffic interlock surface, yet it mutates DOM (visibility, lock, z-order) outside the command system, splitting the source of truth between the history stack and the live DOM. That split is the root cause of findings 1-3 and is the single most important thing to fix. Theming is half-built and dishonest: atrium.ts is dead, CSS vars are hand-copied, and several components hardcode rgba/oklch literals (findings 4,5,8), so the advertised theme switcher would visibly break today. Testability is mediocre — there are good data-role/data-testid hooks, but index-based keys and the index-based active-layer model make reorder/delete behavior hard to assert deterministically. Verdict: salvageable. Fix the command-vs-DOM split in LayersPanel, switch active-layer tracking to element identity, make icons use currentColor, and either wire or delete atrium.ts; no rewrite warranted.

confirmedHighSev.title: Free-transform rotate on a non-<g> element drops its existing translate/scale/matrix transform
confirmedHighSev.impact: Any non-group element whose transform carries translation or scale — notably MuPDF PDF-imported text/paths which arrive as matrix(...) — has that translate/scale thrown away the instant you rotate it with the Q tool. Only the decomposed rotation angle and skew are preserved; the element jumps to a wrong position/size. This is silent geometry corruption that persists into export.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: 1) File > Import PDF, choosing a PDF with text (text=text mode yields editable <text> elements carrying matrix/scale transforms). 2) Switch to the Free Transform tool (press Q). 3) Click a single imported text or path element to select it. 4) Drag from just outside a corner to rotate it. Observe: the moment rotation begins, the element jumps to a wrong position and changes size (scale lost), because its translate/scale transform is replaced by a rotate-only transform. The corruption survives mouse-up and persists into export. (By contrast, rotating a <g> group works correctly.)
confirmedHighSev.reasoning:
Confirmed by reading the code and a numeric reproduction. In freeTransformTool.ts onMouseMove, the rotate branch (lines 191-204) splits on el.tagName === 'g'. Groups compose rotation with the original matrix correctly (multiplyMatrix(rotM, origM)). But for ALL non-<g> elements the else branch (lines 199-203) rebuilds the transform from scratch as `rotate(baseAngle+degrees, cx, cy)` plus skew, where baseAngle = decomposeMatrix(parseTransform(origTransform)).rotate. decomposeMatrix (matrix.ts:70-103) returns translateX/translateY/scaleX/scaleY too, but the rotate branch uses ONLY .rotate. The element's translate and scale components are silently discarded — the original transform string is fully replaced, not preserved.

The auditor's premise about MuPDF-imported content is sound: pdfImport.ts flattenAndScalePdfLayer (lines 79-98) prepends `scale(s)` (and a flattened wrapper transform) to each top-level imported child's transform, and MuPDF's SVG device emits matrix(...) transforms on <text>/<path> glyph elements. These are non-<g> elements that carry translate+scale, so they hit the buggy branch.

Reachability is confirmed: onMouseDown only requires sel.length === 1 with no tag restriction (line 142), so rotating an imported <text> or <path> triggers it. The bad attribute is then committed as an undoable ModifyAttributeCommand in onMouseUp (lines 228-247) and persists to the document/export.

Numeric proof: an element with transform matrix(2,0,0,2,300,400), rotated 30deg about (310,410), is rewritten to `rotate(30.00, 310.00, 410.00)`. Its origin point (0,0) moves from (300,400) to (246.5,-100.1) and its scale collapses from 2x to 1x. This is exactly the position+size jump the finding describes.

Severity adjustment: this is genuine silent geometry corruption affecting a common workflow (rotating imported PDF text/paths), but it is tool-scoped and recoverable via undo (not data loss, crash, or security). High rather than critical.

confirmedHighSev.title: Reflect H/V uses a doc-space AABB center against local-space attributes for transformed elements
confirmedHighSev.impact: getElementAABB() returns the transform-applied (doc-space) bounding box, but the new x/y/d/points are computed in the element's local attribute space. For any rect/text/image/path/polyline that carries a transform (rotation, translate, scale, or PDF matrix()), Flip Horizontal/Vertical places the element in the wrong location — it reflects across the wrong axis. Only works correctly for untransformed elements. The <g> branch is fine (it composes a scale transform), exposing the inconsistency.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: 1) Draw a rect. 2) Press Q (free transform) and rotate it ~30 degrees (or drag-translate it so it carries a transform; rotation is easiest to see). 3) Open the context menu / Object menu and choose Flip Horizontal. confirmedHighSev.title: Ruler drag-to-guide emits guides on the wrong coordinate axis
confirmedHighSev.impact: Dragging a guide off either ruler places it at a meaningless position (the orthogonal coordinate). Guides land far from where the user dropped them; the feature is effectively unusable.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: Open the app at localhost:5173, ensure rulers are visible. Pan/zoom so viewBox.x and viewBox.y differ (or use a non-square page). Mouse-down on the top horizontal ruler and drag downward onto the canvas, releasing over the canvas area. A horizontal (dashed cyan) guide appears, but its Y position equals the document X-coordinate under the cursor instead of the Y where you dropped it — the guide is offset from the drop point. Repeat on the left vertical ruler dragging rightward: the vertical guide's X equals the document Y-coordinate, landing in the wrong place. Note: handleMouseUp is bound to the ruler canvas element, so the release must register the mouseup with React's synthetic handler; when it fires, the placement is wrong as described.
confirmedHighSev.reasoning: Confirmed by reading src/components/Ruler.tsx, src/model/guides.ts, and src/components/Canvas.tsx. In HRuler.handleMouseUp (Ruler.tsx:151-162) the drag-off-ruler branch computes docX = viewBox.x + (px/canvasSize)*viewBox.width where px = e.clientX - rect.left — i.e. the document X coordinate under the mouse's horizontal position — then calls addGuide('h', round(docX)). But guides.ts defines Guide.position as a plain number and Canvas.tsx:186-190 renders an 'h' guide with y1=y2=guide.position. So an 'h' guide's position MUST be a Y coordinate, yet HRuler feeds it an X coordinate. To place a horizontal guide at the drop point it should derive the value from e.clientY against the vertical viewBox span, not e.clientX against the horizontal span. VRuler.handleMouseUp (Ruler.tsx:272-281) is symmetrically wrong: it computes docY from e.clientY and calls addGuide('v', docY), but Canvas.tsx:192-194 renders a 'v' guide as x1=x2=guide.position (an X coordinate). The code's own comments at lines 159-160 explicitly flag this as a placeholder ('we need doc coords / For now, create at a position derived from cursor'), corroborating it was never finished. The orthogonal-axis mapping makes dropped guides land at a meaningless coordinate in the general case (non-square doc, panned/zoomed view). This is a genuine correctness defect, not a false positive.

confirmedHighSev.title: Keyboard shortcuts fire while a <select> dropdown is focused (input guard misses SELECT and contentEditable)
confirmedHighSev.impact: User opens a Properties dropdown, presses Backspace/Delete or an arrow to navigate options, and instead deletes/nudges the selected element. Ctrl+C/V also leak. This is a recurrence of the known 'inputs swallowing/leaking shortcuts' fault-line, on the other side (input leaking into editor).
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: 1. npm run dev, open localhost:5173. 2. Draw a rectangle and select it (Properties panel appears on the right). 3. Click the stroke "Cap" or "Join" dropdown (or Font family on a text element) so the <select> is focused. 4a. Press Delete or Backspace -> the selected shape is deleted from the canvas instead of doing nothing in the dropdown. 4b. Alternatively press an Arrow key -> the shape nudges 1px instead of navigating dropdown options. 4c. Press Ctrl+D / Ctrl+G etc. -> duplicate/group fires on the selection.

Confirmed by reading the code. The global keydown guard in src/model/EditorContext.tsx:58-59 is `const tag = (e.target as HTMLElement)?.tagName; if (tag === 'INPUT' || tag === 'TEXTAREA') return` — it does NOT exclude `<select>` (tagName 'SELECT') or contentEditable. The same handler (lines 122-138) processes ArrowUp/Down/Left/Right (nudgeSelection) and Delete/Backspace (RemoveElementCommand) with e.preventDefault(), gated only on getSelection().length > 0.

PropertiesPanel.tsx renders exactly 7 native `<select>` elements (lines 459, 523, 607, 649, 661, 686, 702: font-family, two fill-type selects, dash, linecap, linejoin, marker start/end), and these only render when an element is selected, so getSelection() is always non-empty when a select is visible. None of the selects has onKeyDown/stopPropagation (only the PropertyInput <input> at line 82 has a key handler), so their keydown events bubble to the window listener. isKeyboardCaptured() (src/tools/registry.ts) is only true during text-editing capture and is NOT set by focusing a select, so it does not mitigate; the single-key guard at line 63 also short-circuits only when captured.

Real browser behavior: with a focused (closed) select, ArrowUp/Down would natively change the option, but the window handler's preventDefault suppresses that and nudges the SVG shape instead. Delete/Backspace have no competing native select behavior, so they unconditionally delete the selected element — a genuine data-loss path. Ctrl+C/X/V/D/G also fire. useToolShortcuts.ts (lines 8-9) has the identical incomplete guard, so single-key tool shortcuts also leak.

I refute the auditor only on the universality of arrow-key leakage when a select's popup is fully expanded (some browsers consume those events in the popup), but the closed-focused state — the dominant interaction — and the Delete/Backspace case are unconditional. Severity high is justified by the data-loss path (deleting the selected element while adjusting its properties).

confirmedHighSev.title: New bold/italic overlay text always renders as Carlito-Regular (multi-slot registry exists but is never populated)
confirmedHighSev.impact: Every user-authored bold or italic text run in a graft/mixed export renders in upright regular weight. The makeFontRegistry multi-slot routing (graftExport.fontRegistry.test.ts) is fully built and tested but receives only one slot in production. Source-text edits keep their original face (gatherSourceFontSlots), so this only bites NEW text — but that is the common 'add a bold heading' case.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: Cannot reproduce through normal UI (no bold/italic control exists). Code-level / edge repro: open a single source PDF (so the graft engine is selected), then add to a source-linked (mixed) layer a <text> element carrying font-weight="bold" or font-style="italic" with a non-source family such as Arial (e.g. via SVG import/paste of such a fragment), then Export to PDF. The run renders in upright regular Carlito instead of bold/italic. Verifiable directly at the unit level by calling makeFontRegistry([Carlito normal/normal slot], 'VfCarlito').resolveFontKey('Arial','italic','bold') and observing it returns 'VfCarlito'.
confirmedHighSev.reasoning:
The mechanical claim is fully verified in code. fileio.ts:28-35 loads Carlito-Italic and Carlito-Bold bytes, but exportPdfBytes (fileio.ts:214-215) passes only { carlito } (regular) to exportViaGraft, and ExportViaGraftOpts (graftExport.ts:76-83) has no italic/bold field. ensureFontIfNeeded (graftExport.ts:375-386) registers exactly one Carlito slot tagged weight:'normal', style:'normal'. makeFontRegistry.resolveFontKey (graftExport.ts:542-555) walks three match rules then returns fallbackKey; for a NEW text run with an unknown family (e.g. 'Arial') in bold/italic, no slot's family matches, so it returns the regular-Carlito fallbackKey. gatherSourceFontSlots (graftExport.ts:402+) only feeds slots for MODIFIED source-text elements, never new content, so new bold/italic text genuinely has only the one normal/normal slot to resolve against. collectTextRuns (graftCs.ts:358-360,389-392) does read font-weight/font-style off the text/tspan and pass them to resolveFontKey, confirming the data path. So a bold/italic attribute on new graft-layer text WOULD silently downgrade to upright regular Carlito.

However, the IMPACT is materially overstated. The auditor calls 'add a bold heading' the common case, but the running app has NO way to author bold or italic on a text element: textTool.ts:226-231 sets only font-family/font-size/fill on new text, and PropertiesPanel.tsx:453-491 exposes only Family, Size, and Letter-spacing for text — there is no bold/italic toggle anywhere, and FONT_FAMILIES (PropertiesPanel.tsx:25+) lists no bold/italic faces. The graft engine also only runs when every layer is source-PDF-backed (shouldUseGraftEngine, fileio.ts:187-200), so the only way to hit this is text carrying an explicit font-weight='bold'/font-style='italic' that originated outside the app (e.g. an imported/pasted SVG fragment placed on a mixed layer). That is a real but narrow path; degradation is graceful (correct glyphs, wrong weight/slant), not a crash or data loss. It is best characterized as a dormant/latent gap: the multi-slot routing is built and tested but starved of bold/italic slots in production, and it has no UI trigger today. It becomes a genuine user-visible bug the moment a bold/italic control is added. High severity is not warranted; low is appropriate.

confirmedHighSev.title: Deleting a background-PDF layer never removes its bytes/source-entry from SourcePdfStore
confirmedHighSev.impact: After importing a background PDF and deleting its layer, the original ~10MB PDF bytes stay pinned in the store for the document's lifetime (memory leak). Worse, the orphaned background entry still keys by the old layer name; re-importing a PDF whose name sanitizes to the same key, or re-adding a layer with that data-src-layer-id, makes the graft engine clone content from the wrong/deleted source. Undo of the delete also won't re-tie state correctly.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: Memory leak (the real consequence): 1) Open/start a document. 2) File menu -> "Open as Background Layer…", choose a large (~10MB) PDF. A new bottom layer appears. 3) In the Layers panel, delete that background layer. 4) In devtools console evaluate the active SourcePdfStore (e.g. via getActiveSourcePdfStore().backgrounds) — the map still contains the entry with its full `bytes` Uint8Array despite the layer being gone, and it persists for the document lifetime (no UI action clears it short of a new primary PDF import). The "wrong-source clone" and "broken undo" scenarios in the finding do NOT reproduce.
confirmedHighSev.reasoning:
The mechanical claim is verified. LayersPanel.tsx:97-103 deleteLayer() executes only `new RemoveElementCommand(editor.doc, layers[idx].element)` and never calls store.removeBackground(layerName). SourcePdfStore.removeBackground (sourcePdf.ts:42) is confirmed dead in production: grep shows it is referenced only in sourcePdf.ts itself and sourcePdf.test.ts. Background imports store a FULL forked copy of the PDF bytes (readAndForkPdfBytes -> retained = arrayBuffer.slice(0), pdfImport.ts:156-159) into store.backgrounds keyed by sanitized layer name (pdfImport.ts:250). Deleting the background layer removes the DOM element but leaves that byte copy pinned for the document lifetime, only cleared by clearAll() on a new primary import. So the memory-leak impact (~full PDF size per deleted background layer) is REAL and accurately sized.

However the auditor materially OVERSTATED the rest of the impact: (1) "graft engine clones content from the wrong/deleted source" is not reachable. After deletion the layer's DOM and its data-src-layer-id children are gone, so classifyLayer/lookupSourceEntry (graftClassify.ts:64, sourceTagging.ts:103-106) never see the deleted layer. A same-name re-import calls addBackground which OVERWRITES the stale key (sourcePdf.ts:38-40, Map.set), so no wrong-source result occurs. Producing a wrong-source clone would require hand-crafting a layer with a colliding data-src-layer-id, not a normal UI flow. (2) "Undo won't re-tie state correctly" is backwards: because the entry is never removed, undoing the delete restores the layer with the same data-source-pdf-id and the still-present store entry is exactly what the graft path needs, so undo is correct; the leak coincidentally aids undo. (3) While ANY background exists, shouldUseGraftEngine (fileio.ts:188) returns false (store.backgrounds.size > 0 forces the pdf-lib path), so the leaked entry has no export-correctness consequence at all — it is purely wasted memory.

Net: a genuine but bounded resource leak, not a high-severity correctness/data-integrity bug. Severity reduced from high to medium.

confirmedHighSev.title: Open SVG / New Document leave stale SourcePdfStore.primary set
confirmedHighSev.impact: Sequence: Open PDF (sets store.primary + ~10MB bytes) → Open SVG → store.primary still references the discarded PDF. Today this is masked because the freshly-imported SVG layers carry no data-src tags so classifyLayer returns 'overlay' and exportPdf falls back to pdf-lib (fileio.ts:188-199). But the bytes leak, and the routing is one stray data-src attribute away from grafting from a document that no longer exists. The store's own doc-comment claims 'a fresh primary import replaces the whole document' — Open SVG is also a whole-document replace and is not covered.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: 1. File > Open PDF... and import A.pdf (sets store.primary to A's bytes; primary layer tagged data-source-pdf-id="__primary__"). 2. Separately, ensure you have B.svg that was produced by File > Export SVG from a document that had imported B.pdf (such an SVG still carries data-source-pdf-id="__primary__" because exportSvgString does not strip source tags). 3. File > Open SVG... and choose B.svg. The canvas now shows B's content, but store.primary still holds A.pdf bytes. 4. File > Export PDF. classifyLayer resolves __primary__ to the stale A entry, shouldUseGraftEngine returns true, and the exported PDF grafts page bytes from A.pdf instead of rendering B -> wrong/cross-document content in the output. (Quick variant to prove statefulness without crafting B: Open PDF A.pdf, then Open SVG any plain SVG, then inspect getActiveSourcePdfStore().primary in devtools -> still non-null pointing at A.)
confirmedHighSev.reasoning:

SourcePdfStore.clearPrimary()/reset() (sourcePdf.ts:34,61) are production dead code; the only path that clears the store is recordImportedSource('primary') -> clearAll() (sourcePdf.ts:84-86), invoked only from pdfImport.ts. importSvg (fileio.ts:451) -> applyParsedSvg is wired to the "Open SVG..." menu (App.tsx:154) and replaces the whole document in place without resetting the store, so store.primary keeps the bytes of a previously-Opened PDF.

The auditor actually UNDERSTATED reachability. The masking they describe (classifyLayer returns 'overlay' when a layer has no data-source-pdf-id, so shouldUseGraftEngine falls back to pdf-lib) is real, BUT exportSvgString (fileio.ts:103-122) only strips [data-role=...] overlay elements; it does NOT strip data-source-pdf-id / data-src-* tags. So an SVG saved by vectorfeld itself from imported-PDF content retains data-source-pdf-id="__primary__" on its layers. Re-opening such an SVG via "Open SVG..." while store.primary still holds an UNRELATED prior PDF makes classifyLayer (graftClassify.ts) call lookupSourceEntry(store,'__primary__') -> store.getPrimary() (sourceTagging.ts:103-105) which returns the STALE entry. shouldUseGraftEngine then returns true and exportViaGraft grafts page bytes from a document that is no longer open -> silent cross-document content corruption/leak in the exported PDF, not merely a "one stray attribute away" hypothetical.

The memory leak (~10MB retained bytes) is a minor secondary effect. The "New Document" portion of the title is NOT substantiated: there is no New Document command in App.tsx; the app is single-document and Open SVG mutates the existing doc in place. So the title is partly inaccurate, but the substantive defect (Open SVG leaves stale primary, which is graft-reachable via SVG round-trip) holds. High severity is appropriate for a silent wrong-document export; not critical because it requires the specific Open-PDF-then-Open-a-source-tagged-SVG sequence and produces a wrong export rather than crash/security breach.

confirmedHighSev.title: pdf-lib fallback drops rotation, skew, and non-uniform shear on every non-text element
confirmedHighSev.impact: Any rotated rect/ellipse/circle/image in the document exports unrotated and mis-placed via the pdf-lib path (background composites, freshly authored docs). drawPath is fine (full matrix applied to every point); the primitives are not. Word/Designer PDFs with rotated logos/photos export wrong.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: In the running app (localhost:5173) start a fresh/blank document (so no source PDF → forces the pdf-lib fallback engine). Draw a rectangle (or ellipse/place an image). Select it, use the Free Transform tool (Q) or Select tool rotate handle to rotate it ~30-45°. Click Export PDF. Open the exported PDF: the shape appears axis-aligned (unrotated) and shifted from where it sat on canvas, instead of rotated. A rotated path drawn the same way exports correctly, demonstrating the primitive-vs-path divergence.

CONFIRMED. extractScale() (src/model/pdfExport.ts:115) returns only sx=√(a²+b²), sy=√(c²+d²) — pure column magnitudes that discard the rotation angle and shear. For a pure rotation matrix [cos,sin,-sin,cos,e,f], multiplyMatrix composes it into ctx.matrix, and extractScale returns sx=sy=1. drawRect/drawEllipseEl/drawCircleEl/drawImage size the shape via this scale and place it by passing ONE corner/center through svgPtToPdf, then call pdf-lib drawRectangle/drawEllipse/drawCircle/drawImage with NO rotate parameter. Result: the shape is drawn axis-aligned — rotation dropped AND position wrong (box is laid out axis-aligned from a corner that was correctly rotated). drawPath is correctly handled because transformPathD applies the full matrix to every point; the finding accurately distinguishes this.

Production reachability is genuine — the header comment ("production exportPdf continues to use the svg2pdf path") is STALE. fileio.ts exportPdfBytes (the real production path called by App.tsx Export PDF) routes to svgStringToPdfBytes (the pdf-lib engine) whenever shouldUseGraftEngine returns false: i.e. no source PDF (freshly authored docs) or any background composite present. Imported single-source PDFs go through the graft engine (graftCs.ts, which explicitly preserves rotation), so those are unaffected — which is why severity is confined to the fallback engine rather than catastrophic.

Real-world trigger is concrete: freeTransformTool.ts:196-203 and selectTool rotate mode set transform="rotate(angle,cx,cy)" directly on elements with position attributes (rect/ellipse/circle/image), and matrixToString(rotateMatrix...) on groups. A user who draws a rect, rotates it, and exports gets a wrong PDF via the pdf-lib path. High is the appropriate severity: it is a real, visible mis-render of common content in a production code path, but bounded to the non-graft (authored/composite) engine.

confirmedHighSev.title: Documented 'text content tracked at Command level' contract is unwired (commandTouchesSource consumed nowhere)
confirmedHighSev.impact: isElementModified is attribute-only by design and explicitly defers text-content edits to a Command signal that is never read. There is also no text-content edit command in commands.ts (textTool only ADDS new overlay text). The contract is fiction. When Phase-3 in-place source-text editing lands (mutating an existing source <text>'s textContent without changing attributes), isElementModified returns false, findModifiedSourceElements omits it, classifyLayer returns 'graft', and export grafts the PRISTINE source bytes — the user's text edit is silently lost on PDF export.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: Not reproducible in the running app: no UI mutates an existing imported source <text> element's textContent. To demonstrate the latent gap in a test instead: import a source PDF page (snapshotImportedElements stamps data-src-* on a <text>), set that text element's textContent to a new string WITHOUT changing any attribute, then call classifyLayer(layer, store) and observe it returns kind:'graft' (not 'mixed') — so an export would graft pristine source bytes and drop the textContent change. This becomes a live data-loss bug only if/when an in-place source-text-content editing command is added without also wiring textContent into isElementModified or consuming commandTouchesSource in classifyLayer.
confirmedHighSev.reasoning:
The finding's factual claims are all verified, but its severity (high, "user's text edit silently lost") is overstated because the triggering operation is unreachable in the current product.

VERIFIED FACTS:

- The doc comment at sourceSnapshot.ts:17-20 claims textContent changes are "tracked at the Command level (see Command.touchesSource)".
- commandTouchesSource / .touchesSource() (commands.ts:22-24) is consumed ONLY inside commands.ts itself (CompoundCommand.touchesSource ORs its children, line 318) and in commands.test.ts. graftClassify.ts:58-80 (classifyLayer, the sole real consumer of the modified/new/removed detection, called from graftExport.ts:100 and fileio.ts:190) never imports or calls commandTouchesSource. So the documented contract is genuinely unwired.
- classifyLayer's gate (line 75) returns 'graft' (pristine source bytes) when findModifiedSourceElements, collectNewLeaves, and findRemovedElementBboxes are all empty. A pure-textContent mutation of a tagged source <text> would: (a) not change attributes -> not in modifiedElements; (b) still carry data-src-* -> skipped by collectNewLeaves (!isFromSource guard, graftClassify.ts:92); (c) keep count and remain in DOM -> not removed. Result: 'graft', edit lost. The mechanism the finding describes is logically real.

WHY IT DOES NOT MANIFEST: There is no code path that mutates an existing source <text> element's textContent. The only textContent assignments outside tests (grep across src) are: textTool.ts (a brand-new element it just created via AddElementCommand, which is an untagged overlay leaf correctly caught by collectNewLeaves -> 'mixed' -> overlay-rendered, no loss), measureTool's own preview, and Canvas wireframe style. The finding assumed Phase-3 in-place source-text editing is "future"; the worklog (eb0-shipped) shows Phase-3 shipped, BUT eb0 only changed HOW already-detected modified text is re-rendered (source font vs Carlito) — it did not add a textContent-only edit operation or a detector for one. InspectorPanel only reads textContent for a display label.

CONCLUSION: A real documentation-vs-implementation gap and a genuine latent footgun for any future in-place source-text-content edit feature, but not a bug that manifests in the running app today because the triggering edit does not exist. Downgrade high -> low (latent/contract-doc issue, no user-reachable data loss).

confirmedHighSev.title: Paste re-IDs only the top element; transferred descendants keep original ids → duplicate ids in document
confirmedHighSev.impact: After pasting any element that has children with ids (groups, multi-tspan PDF text, compound shapes), the document contains duplicate ids. doc.getElement(id) uses svg.querySelector('#'+id) (document.ts:88) which silently returns the FIRST match, so later selection-by-id, layer lookups, and graft/export keyed on ids resolve to the wrong element. Duplicate ids also make exported SVG/PDF non-conformant.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: In the running app (localhost:5173): 1) Draw two rectangles. 2) Select both and press Ctrl+G to group them (group gets a fresh id; each rect keeps its original vf-N id). 3) With the group selected, press Ctrl+C then Ctrl+V (or Ctrl+D to duplicate). 4) Inspect the SVG (e.g. via export or devtools): the pasted group has a new id, but its two child rects carry the SAME ids as the original group's child rects — duplicate ids now exist in the document. Confirm wrong-element resolution by calling doc.getElement('<duplicated-child-id>') — it returns the original child, not the pasted one. Exported SVG/PDF will also contain duplicate id attributes.
confirmedHighSev.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the code. In pasteClipboard (src/model/clipboard.ts), only the top element gets a fresh id: attrs.id = generateId() at line 76, applied to the AddElementCommand-built element. The descendants are then transferred verbatim from the re-parsed clipboard original via `while (original.firstChild) { created.appendChild(original.firstChild) }` (lines 92-94). Those descendants retain the id="vf-N" attributes that copySelection() serialized (XMLSerializer at line 21 preserves all attributes). sanitizeSvgTree (src/model/fileio.ts:58) only strips dangerous tags and on*/href attributes — it does NOT strip ids, so child ids survive. Children genuinely carry ids: addElement (document.ts:58-62) assigns a generateId() id to every created element, and grouping (EditorContext.tsx:92-103) moves those id-bearing elements into a new group without re-IDing them. So pasting a copied group (the original still in the document) yields child elements whose ids duplicate the originals. The impact path is real: doc.getElement (document.ts:88) does svg.querySelector('#'+CSS.escape(id)) which returns only the FIRST match, so any id-keyed lookup after paste can resolve to the wrong (original) element, and exported SVG/PDF contains duplicate ids (non-conformant). The existing clipboard.test.ts only tests a flat rect with no children, so it passes while masking this bug. confirmedHighSev.title: GroupCommand undo re-parents children to sel[0]'s parent, not their original parents (cross-layer group corrupts layers)
confirmedHighSev.impact: Group elements from two layers, then undo: every grouped element is dumped into the first element's layer. The other layer silently loses its content; undo does not restore the prior document structure. Data/structure corruption that survives further edits and export.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: 1) Create two layers (Layer A and Layer B), each with at least one shape. Ensure both are unlocked and visible. 2) Use the select tool to drag a marquee that intersects shapes on BOTH layers (this is the only way to select across layers — verify selection count includes elements from both). 3) Press Ctrl+G to group. The group is created in Layer A (sel[0]'s parent) and Layer B's shape(s) get moved into it. 4) Press Ctrl+Z to undo. Observe: the shape that originated in Layer B is now placed in Layer A, not back in Layer B. Inspect the SVG/layer panel: Layer B has lost its original content; document structure is not restored to its pre-group state.
confirmedHighSev.reasoning: Code confirms the defect exactly as described. GroupCommand (src/model/commands.ts:223-255) captures a single `parent` in its constructor (line 230-231) and its undo() (lines 244-250) re-parents EVERY child to that one `parent` via `this.parent.insertBefore(child, this.group)`. It does not track per-child original parents. A selection can legitimately span multiple layers: marquee completion in src/tools/selectTool.ts:694-713 iterates over ALL `g[data-layer-name]` layers (skipping only locked/hidden), collecting children from every layer into one `hits` array passed to setSelection. The two Ctrl+G call sites (src/App.tsx:226-235 and src/model/EditorContext.tsx:92-103) both pass `sel[0].parentElement` as the single parent and the full multi-layer selection, with no same-layer guard. Therefore after grouping a cross-layer selection and undoing, all formerly cross-layer children are dumped into sel[0]'s layer instead of being restored to their original layers — undo is not a faithful inverse and the original document structure is permanently lost, surviving further edits and export. Existing tests (commandsNew.test.ts:121-184) only exercise the single-parent case, so this is uncovered. Note: execute() itself necessarily consolidates children into one layer (inherent to placing them in one <g>); the genuine bug is the non-restorative undo, which is a real structure-corruption defect. High severity is warranted: undo/redo correctness and layer integrity are core invariants of a vector editor and the corruption is silent and persistent.

confirmedHighSev.title: Layer visibility/lock toggles bypass command history: not undoable, not dirty, but DO affect export

Observe: the TopBar tab dirty dot (data-role=tab-dirty-dot) does NOT appear and StatusBar still shows green Saved. Press Ctrl+Z — the layer stays hidden (not undoable). Then File > Export SVG (or Export PDF/PNG) and inspect the output: the hidden layer's <g> carries style="display:none" and its content is missing from the rendered/exported file, with no warning.
confirmedHighSev.reasoning: Verified all core claims against source. toggleVisibility (LayersPanel.tsx:105-109) sets el.style.display directly and toggleLock (111-116) uses setAttribute/removeAttribute directly; neither calls editor.history.execute(), unlike every sibling op (addLayer/deleteLayer/moveLayerUp/moveLayerDown) in the same file. Consequences confirmed: (1) Export reads live DOM — exportSvgString (fileio.ts:103-104), exportPdf (221-228) and exportPng (257-275) all do doc.svg.cloneNode(true)+serialize; sanitizeSvgTree only strips dangerous tags/attrs and OVERLAY_SELECTOR only strips editor overlays, so a layer <g style="display:none"> is baked into every export. (2) Not undoable — the toggle pushes nothing onto history, so Ctrl+Z cannot restore a hidden layer. (3) No dirty signal — App.tsx:71/73 derives dirty from editor.history.canUndo, which is unchanged by the toggle, so the TopBar dirty dot (TopBar.tsx:158, data-role tab-dirty-dot) never lights. One detail is overstated: the StatusBar green Saved dot (StatusBar.tsx:74-78) is hardcoded #4aa85a with no dirty prop, so it is always green for ALL edits, not a layer-toggle-specific divergence; the real dirty indicator is the TopBar tab dot, which correctly fails to appear. This does not undermine the finding — the visibility path is a genuine silent lost-work/data-divergence trap. Lock toggle is less severe: data-locked is an editor-only, non-rendering attribute, so its export impact is benign though it is likewise non-undoable.

confirmedHighSev.title: addLayer repositions the new layer OUTSIDE the AddElementCommand, so redo restores wrong z-order
confirmedHighSev.impact: Undo then redo of 'add layer' leaves the layer above the overlay (wrong stacking / rendered above selection handles), diverging from the post-create state. Z-order corruption across undo/redo.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: In the running app: open Layers panel, click "+" to add a layer, draw a shape into that layer; then Undo (Ctrl+Z) the add, then Redo (Ctrl+Y/Ctrl+Shift+Z). After redo the layer is appended after the selection/grid/guides overlay groups, so its content renders on top of the selection handles and grid instead of beneath them (DOM order: inspect that the data-layer-name g is the last child of the svg, after data-role="overlay").
confirmedHighSev.reasoning: Verified against source. LayersPanel.tsx:87-92 creates the layer via AddElementCommand (executed through history) and THEN imperatively calls svg.insertBefore(newLayer, overlay) outside the command. document.ts:66 (addElement) uses parent.appendChild, so initial execute appends the new layer to the END of the svg, after the overlay groups; line 92 then moves it before the overlay. The svg child order at init (Canvas.tsx:98-126) is [layer, grid-overlay, user-guides-overlay, guides-overlay, overlay], so the new layer should sit just before the selection overlay. On undo, AddElementCommand.undo() removes the element. On redo, AddElementCommand.execute() takes the this.element branch (commands.ts:96-100) and calls this.parent.appendChild(this.element), re-appending to the END of the svg (after overlay). The insertBefore reposition is NOT part of the command and is never replayed, nor does refreshLayers or anything else re-correct child order. Result: post-redo DOM order diverges from post-create order, leaving the layer above the selection/grid/guides overlays. No test covers this. The defect is genuine. Severity adjusted down from high to medium: a freshly added layer is empty so the redo's visual effect is subtle until content is drawn into the layer, at which point that content occludes selection handles/grid/guides. It is a conditional rendering/z-order divergence, not a crash or data loss.

confirmedHighSev.title: Layer list shown in raw DOM/paint order (bottom layer on top); move-up/down arrows are inverted vs z-order
confirmedHighSev.impact: Every design tool (Illustrator/Figma/Sketch) lists the top-most painted layer at the top. Here it is inverted, and the up/down arrows move layers opposite to what the visual list implies. Users will reorder layers the wrong way and mis-stack content.
confirmedHighSev.reproHint: In the running app (localhost:5173): create a doc with at least 2 layers (click the '+' in the Layers panel). Draw a distinct shape on each layer overlapping the other. Observe in the canvas which shape is painted on top, then look at the Layers panel: the shape painted ON TOP appears as the BOTTOM row (inverted). Select the bottom layer row and click its up arrow (▲): the layer's content moves visually DOWN in the paint stack rather than up — confirming both the list-order inversion and the arrow inversion.
confirmedHighSev.reasoning: Confirmed at code level. document.ts:96-98 getLayerElements() returns Array.from(svg.querySelectorAll('g[data-layer-name]')) = DOM/document order. In SVG, document order IS paint order: earlier siblings paint first (underneath), later siblings paint on top. LayersPanel.tsx:56-70 refreshLayers maps these directly into `layers` with NO .reverse(), and the render (line 192) lists layers[0] as the TOP row. So the top row in the panel is the FIRST DOM element = visually painted at the BOTTOM of the stack — inverted vs every mainstream design tool (Illustrator/Figma/Sketch list top-painted on top). The move arrows compound this: moveLayerUp(idx) (line 118-123) executes ReorderElementCommand(layers[idx].element, layers[idx-1].element) which (commands.ts:201-208) calls parent.insertBefore(element, newNextSibling), moving the element EARLIER in the DOM = further DOWN in paint order. So the up arrow moves content visually down and vice versa. No CSS z-index, no reverse() anywhere counteracts this (grep clean). No test covers ordering semantics. The defect is deterministic and always manifests. Severity adjusted from high to medium: it is a real, universal-convention-violating usability bug that will mislead users into mis-stacking, but it causes no data loss/crash, the arrows are functional (just inverted), and every action is undoable via history — so it is recoverable, making 'high' a slight overstatement.

allFindings.title: Free-transform rotate on a non-<g> element drops its existing translate/scale/matrix transform
allFindings.evidence:
const baseAngle = decomposeMatrix(parseTransform(state.origTransform)).rotate
... let t = `rotate(${(baseAngle + degrees).toFixed(2)}, ${center.x.toFixed(2)}, ${center.y.toFixed(2)})`
t = setSkew(t, existingSkew.skewX, existingSkew.skewY)
el.setAttribute('transform', t)
allFindings.impact: Any non-group element whose transform carries translation or scale — notably MuPDF PDF-imported text/paths which arrive as matrix(...) — has that translate/scale thrown away the instant you rotate it with the Q tool. Only the decomposed rotation angle and skew are preserved; the element jumps to a wrong position/size. This is silent geometry corruption that persists into export.
allFindings.fix: Compose with the full original matrix instead of decomposing and discarding: build rotM = rotateMatrix(degrees, center.x, center.y); origM = parseTransform(state.origTransform); el.setAttribute('transform', matrixToString(multiplyMatrix(rotM, origM))) — the same path already used for tagName==='g'. The g-vs-non-g split here is the bug; both should use matrix composition.

allFindings.title: Reflect H/V uses a doc-space AABB center against local-space attributes for transformed elements
allFindings.impact: getElementAABB() returns the transform-applied (doc-space) bounding box, but the new x/y/d/points are computed in the element's local attribute space. For any rect/text/image/path/polyline that carries a transform (rotation, translate, scale, or PDF matrix()), Flip Horizontal/Vertical places the element in the wrong location — it reflects across the wrong axis. Only works correctly for untransformed elements. The <g> branch is fine (it composes a scale transform), exposing the inconsistency.
allFindings.fix: Compute the center from the element's LOCAL getBBox() (not getElementAABB) for the attribute-rewriting branches, OR for transformed elements fall through to the buildScaleTransform() matrix path used for <g>. Do not mix doc-space center with local-space coordinate rewrites.

allFindings.title: Multi-select scale ignores per-element transforms (anchor stays in doc space, geometry mutated in local space)
allFindings.impact: When two or more elements are selected and any of them has its own transform, the scale anchor (from unionBBox, in doc space) and the mouse point are never mapped into each element's local space, yet scaleElement() writes local attributes (x/width/cx/r/...). Scaling a multi-selection that contains a rotated or translated shape produces wrong sizes/positions for those members. unionBBox is also used as origBBox so sx/sy are derived from a doc-space box while applied to local coords.
allFindings.fix: Per element, inverse-transform the anchor and recompute scale in that element's local frame, or (simpler and consistent) scale every element by composing scaleAroundMatrix into its transform in the shared parent/doc frame rather than editing local geometry attrs.

allFindings.title: Free-transform scale divides by (startMouse - anchor) with no zero/degenerate guard → NaN/Infinity
allFindings.evidence:
const sx = origBBox.width > 0 ? (pt.x - anchor.x) / (state.startMouse.x - anchor.x) : 1
const sy = origBBox.height > 0 ? (pt.y - anchor.y) / (state.startMouse.y - anchor.y) : 1
allFindings.impact: The guard checks origBBox.width/height, not the denominator. If the grabbed corner is (near-)vertically or horizontally aligned with the anchor — e.g. a zero-width/height-ish bbox, or a degenerate line/text bbox — (startMouse.x - anchor.x) can be ~0, yielding sx = Infinity/NaN. That NaN propagates into setAttribute, blanking geometry and producing an invalid undo entry. selectTool's scale path guards this with MIN_BBOX_DIM/MIN_SCALE_SIZE; free-transform does not.
allFindings.fix: Guard the denominator: const denomX = state.startMouse.x - anchor.x; const sx = Math.abs(denomX) > EPS ? (pt.x - anchor.x) / denomX : 1; same for sy. Optionally clamp to a MIN_SCALE like selectTool does.

allFindings.title: selectTool circle scale: r is scaled by (sx+sy)/2 but cx/cy are scaled independently by sx/sy
allFindings.evidence:
const s = (activeSx + activeSy) / 2
el.setAttribute('cx', String(anchorX + (origCx - anchorX) * sx))
el.setAttribute('cy', String(anchorY + (origCy - anchorY) * sy))
el.setAttribute('r', String(origR * s))
allFindings.impact: For a circle inside a multi-selection (or any non-uniform corner drag), the center is repositioned with anisotropic sx/sy while the radius uses the averaged scalar s. The circle drifts off its expected anchor-relative position and its size no longer matches the selection box, so the rendered circle pokes outside / sits inside the selection rectangle during and after scaling.
allFindings.fix: Either convert the circle to an ellipse when scaled non-uniformly, or move cx/cy by the same scalar s used for r so center and radius stay consistent. At minimum document that circles can only scale uniformly and force s on both center deltas.

allFindings.title: Rotate commit is gated by a translational dead-zone (dx/dy of the mouse), discarding valid small-arc rotations
allFindings.impact: The commit gate measures linear mouse displacement, which is the wrong metric for rotation. A rotation performed with the cursor very close to the rotation center (large angular change, tiny linear dx/dy) is silently discarded and the DOM reset — the user rotates the object, releases, and the rotation vanishes. Conversely the metric is meaningless for rotate intent.
allFindings.fix: For mode === 'rotate', gate on accumulated angle delta (e.g. |angleDeg| above a small threshold) rather than on mouse dx/dy. Track the final committed angle in dragState.rotate and check it at mouseup.

allFindings.title: selectTool onMouseUp never refreshes the overlay after committing scale/rotate/move
allFindings.impact: commitChanges() uses the reset-then-execute pattern: it sets attributes back to the original, then ModifyAttributeCommand.execute() re-applies them. The selection overlay (selection box + handles) is rebuilt only by refreshOverlay, which is RAF-coalesced and was last triggered mid-drag. After commit there is no explicit refresh, so handles can momentarily sit at stale positions until the next mouse event triggers updateOverlay. Mostly cosmetic but visible on fast release.
allFindings.fix: Call refreshOverlaySync() at the end of onMouseUp after commit, mirroring the zoom path in Canvas.tsx which already uses refreshOverlaySync() for immediate visual consistency.

allFindings.title: Rotation matrix decomposition is approximate; rotate() string baseAngle can fight matrix-decomposed baseAngle across tools
allFindings.evidence:
freeTransform: const baseAngle = decomposeMatrix(parseTransform(state.origTransform)).rotate
selectTool: const rotMatch = origT.match(/rotate\(([-\d.]+)/); const baseAngle = rotMatch ? parseFloat(rotMatch[1]) : 0
allFindings.impact: The two tools derive the existing rotation differently — free-transform via QR matrix decomposition, selectTool via a regex on the literal rotate(...) string. An element rotated in one tool then rotated in the other can accumulate small drift or read a different baseAngle (e.g. a rotate() string written by selectTool vs a matrix() composed by a group op). decomposeMatrix's skewX/sign handling is also lossy for combined skew+rotation. Inconsistent base-angle sources make round-tripping fragile.
allFindings.fix: Standardize on matrix composition for rotation in both tools (multiplyMatrix(rotM, origM)) and stop parsing rotate() substrings. This also subsumes finding select-transform-1.

allFindings.title: Shift-constrained scale uses Math.max(sx, sy) of signed values, breaking uniform scale when one axis is mirrored
allFindings.impact: sx/sy here are always positive (derived from Math.abs(localPt-anchor)/width), so the sign issue is mild, but Math.max of magnitudes means dragging a corner inward (shrink) snaps to the larger ratio, so uniform-shrink feels like it tracks the wrong axis. freeTransform uses Math.sign(sx)*Math.max(|sx|,|sy|) which preserves mirroring; the two tools behave differently under Shift.
allFindings.fix: Use the same Shift-uniform formula in both tools; prefer magnitude-max with sign preservation as freeTransform does, and pick the axis the user is actively dragging rather than unconditional max.

allFindings.title: directSelectTool uses a second, incompatible path parser that mangles relative commands and drops H/V/S/Q/T/A
allFindings.evidence: parsePathWithHandles / parsePathAnchors / updatePathAnchor all use `const re = /([MLCZmlcz])\s*.../g` and then do e.g. `if (cmd === 'M' || cmd === 'm' ...)` treating the relative variant IDENTICALLY to absolute: `result.push({ pos: { x: values[i], y: values[i + 1] } ...})`. There is NO accumulation of current point for lowercase commands. The regex matches only MLCZ — H,V,S,Q,T,A are not matched at all. In updatePathAnchor the same regex collects `segments`, and the rebuild `segments.map(s => ... `${s.cmd} ${s.coords.join(' ')}`)` re-emits whatever was matched and SILENTLY OMITS any H/V/S/Q/T/A run that the regex skipped.
allFindings.impact: Direct-selecting/dragging a node on any path containing relative segments places anchors at absurd absolute positions (and the inverse delta math in updatePathAnchor then corrupts the d). Direct-selecting a path with H/V/S/Q/T/A (extremely common in imported SVGs and in paths produced by the app's own shapeToPath / convert-to-path) and then moving ANY node rebuilds the d with those segments deleted — permanent geometry loss committed via ModifyAttributeCommand. Note the rest of the app (selectTool, freeTransformTool, knife, joinPaths, pdfExport) uses the robust parsePathD which DOES normalize all of these; so a shape converted to a path and then node-edited gets silently destroyed.
allFindings.fix: Delete the bespoke regex parser. Rebuild parsePathAnchors/updatePathAnchor/parsePathWithHandles/updatePathControlPoint on top of parsePathD()+commandsToD() (which already produce absolute M/L/C/Z). Edit the structured PathCommand array and re-serialize, so all command types round-trip correctly.

allFindings.title: Auto-convert-to-path in direct-select holds a stale element ref across undo
allFindings.evidence: On clicking a non-path the tool does `getHistory().execute(compound)` (Remove old + Add new path), then `const newPath = addCmd.getElement(); ... state.selectedPath = newPath; showAnchors(svg, newPath)`. state.selectedPath now references the freshly-added DOM node.
